cards.front: {{c1::Competition}} is an interaction in which individuals use a resource in short supply, so that each lowers the survival, growth or reproduction of the others.
cards.back: The resource can be food, water, light, nutrients or space.
cards.quote: Competition is an interaction in which individuals use a resource in short supply, so that each lowers the survival, growth or reproduction of the others.

cards.front: How does exploitation competition differ from interference competition?
cards.back: Exploitation is indirect: each competitor uses up a resource, leaving less for the other. Interference is direct: one individual acts on another by fighting, overgrowing or holding a territory.
cards.quote: In exploitation competition the effect is indirect: each competitor uses up a resource, leaving less for the other.

cards.front: On a reef, one coral species grows over a neighbouring colony of a different coral species and shades it. Which kinds of competition are these, by route and by species?
cards.back: Interference competition (direct action, by overgrowing), and interspecific, since the two corals are different species.
cards.quote: In interference competition one individual acts directly on another, by fighting, overgrowing, or holding a territory.

cards.front: State the invasion test for stable coexistence of two competitors.
cards.back: Each species must be able to grow when it is rare and the other sits at its carrying capacity (the size it would settle at alone).
cards.quote: Two competitors coexist stably when each can grow when it is rare and the other sits at its carrying capacity

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, dN1/dt = r1 N1 [1 - (N1 + {{c1::alpha12 N2}}) / K1].
cards.back: Species 2's numbers, converted into species 1 units, add to species 1's own crowding.
cards.quote: dN1/dt = r1 N1 [1 - (N1 + alpha12 N2) / K1]
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, what does the coefficient alpha12 measure?
cards.back: The effect of one species 2 individual on species 1, measured in species 1 individuals. Swapping the subscripts is the usual mix-up.
cards.quote: is the effect of one species 2 individual on species 1, measured in species 1 individuals.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: In a Lotka-Volterra competition model, alpha12 = 0.25. How many species 2 individuals crowd species 1 as much as one species 1 individual?
cards.back: Four. Each species 2 individual counts as 0.25 of a species 1 individual, so 1 / 0.25 = 4.
cards.quote: If alpha12 = 0.5, two individuals of species 2 crowd species 1 as much as one of its own.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: An {{c1::isocline}} is the line where a species' growth is zero.
cards.quote: An isocline is the line where a species' growth is zero.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: In a Lotka-Volterra system with K1 = 100 and alpha12 = 0.5, why does species 1's isocline meet the N2 axis at 200 rather than 100?
cards.back: With N1 = 0, species 1's growth is zero when 0.5 N2 = 100, so N2 = K1 / alpha12 = 200. Each species 2 individual fills only half the room of a species 1 individual.
cards.quote: For species 1 it is N1 + 0.5 N2 = 100, running from N1 = 100 on its own axis to N2 = 200.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition: r1 = 0.5 and r2 = 0.25 per day, K1 = 100, K2 = 80, alpha12 = alpha21 = 0.5. Now N1 = N2 = 60. Find dN1/dt and dN2/dt.
cards.back: dN1/dt = 0.5 x 60 x [1 - (60 + 30)/100] = 3 per day. dN2/dt = 0.25 x 60 x [1 - (30 + 60)/80] = -1.875 per day. Species 1 grows; species 2 declines.
cards.quote: Take r1 = 0.5 per day, r2 = 0.25 per day, K1 = 100 individuals, K2 = 80 individuals, alpha12 = alpha21 = 0.5
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Two species follow the Lotka-Volterra competition model with K1 = 90, K2 = 60 and alpha12 = alpha21 = 0.5. Find the positive equilibrium from the isoclines.
cards.back: Isoclines: N1 + 0.5 N2 = 90 and 0.5 N1 + N2 = 60. Substitute N1 = 90 - 0.5 N2: 45 + 0.75 N2 = 60, so N2 = 20 and N1 = 80.
cards.quote: Substitute N1 = 100 - 0.5 N2 into the second: 50 - 0.25 N2 + N2 = 80, so 0.75 N2 = 30
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition with r1 = 0.4 and r2 = 0.2 per day, K1 = 90, K2 = 60, alpha12 = alpha21 = 0.5. Find each species' per-capita growth rate when rare and the other is at its K.
cards.back: Species 1 rare: 0.4 x (1 - 0.5 x 60/90) = 0.267 per day. Species 2 rare: 0.2 x (1 - 0.5 x 90/60) = 0.05 per day. Both positive, so both pass the invasion test.
cards.quote: Species 1, rare among species 2 at its carrying capacity, grows at 0.5 x (1 - 0.5 x 80/100) = 0.3 per day.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, which two conditions together give stable coexistence?
cards.back: K1 > alpha12 K2 and K2 > alpha21 K1. They are the invasion test, rearranged.
cards.quote: The two coexistence conditions are this same test, rearranged: K1 > alpha12 K2 is 100 > 0.5 x 80 = 40
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Why does "species 1 limits itself more than it limits species 2" equal the condition K2 > alpha21 K1?
cards.back: One species 1 individual fills 1/K1 of its own room and alpha21/K2 of species 2's room. 1/K1 > alpha21/K2; multiplying by K1 K2 gives K2 > alpha21 K1.
cards.quote: Species 1 limits itself more when 1/K1 > alpha21/K2; multiply both sides by K1 K2 to get K2 > alpha21 K1

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, what happens when both coexistence conditions are reversed (K1 < alpha12 K2 and K2 < alpha21 K1)?
cards.back: Each species wins from some starts, so the starting numbers decide which one excludes the other.
cards.quote: each species wins from some starts, so the starting numbers decide

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition with K1 = 100, K2 = 80 and alpha21 = 0.5. How large can alpha12 get before species 1 fails the invasion test?
cards.back: Species 1 passes only while K1 > alpha12 K2, so alpha12 < 100/80 = 1.25. It can exceed 1 and species 1 still passes.
cards.quote: Comparing each alpha with 1 is a tempting shortcut that ignores how much room each species has.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition: K1 = 100, K2 = 150, alpha12 = 0.5, alpha21 = 1.2. A student says species 2 must lose because alpha21 is above 1. Is the student right?
cards.back: No. K1 > alpha12 K2 is 100 > 75, true; K2 > alpha21 K1 is 150 > 120, true. Both pass, so the model predicts stable coexistence.
cards.why: Comparing alpha with 1 ignores how much room (K) each species has.
cards.quote: Comparing each alpha with 1 is a tempting shortcut that ignores how much room each species has.
cards.section: Lotka-Volterra: the invasion test in numbers

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition: K1 = 100, K2 = 120, alpha12 = 1.5, alpha21 = 1.4. What does the model predict?
cards.back: K1 < alpha12 K2 (100 < 180) and K2 < alpha21 K1 (120 < 140): both reversed. Each species wins from some starts; the starting numbers decide.
cards.quote: Both are reversed, K1 < alpha12 K2 and K2 < alpha21 K1: each species wins from some starts

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, can a higher growth rate r decide whether two species coexist or one is excluded?
cards.back: No. r does not appear in the conditions K1 > alpha12 K2 and K2 > alpha21 K1, so it cannot change the verdict. (Only when both conditions are reversed can r shift the line dividing the starts each species wins from.)
cards.quote: Since r is not in the conditions, it cannot change the verdict

cards.front: State the competitive exclusion principle.
cards.back: Two species limited by exactly the same resource cannot coexist indefinitely. Treat it as a model conclusion, not a law.
cards.quote: two species limited by exactly the same resource cannot coexist indefinitely

cards.front: Under what conditions does competitive exclusion follow as a model conclusion?
cards.back: A single limiting resource, a constant and well-mixed environment, populations that settle to a steady state, and nothing else holding the winner down.
cards.quote: It follows when there is a single limiting resource, a constant and well-mixed environment, populations that settle to a steady state

cards.front: Two algae in a lake draw on one nutrient, and in steady lab culture one always excludes the other. In the lake, conditions change with the seasons and a grazer eats whichever alga is commoner. Must exclusion happen in the lake?
cards.back: Not necessarily. The lake breaks the conditions exclusion rests on: the environment is not constant, and a predator hitting the commoner species can hold the winner down.
cards.quote: Real places often break those conditions with several resources, changing seasons, patchy habitat, or predators that hit the commoner species.

cards.front: Gause grew two Paramecium species alone and together. What did he see, and what principle were such results later summed up as?
cards.back: Alone, each grew well; together, P. aurelia persisted and P. caudatum declined toward disappearance. Such results were summed up as the competitive exclusion principle.
cards.quote: together, where P. aurelia persisted and P. caudatum declined toward disappearance

cards.front: What experiment tests whether a competitor keeps a species out of a place it could otherwise live?
cards.back: Remove the competitor and watch whether the species survives there.
cards.quote: To catch a competitor keeping a species out of a place it could otherwise live, take the competitor away and watch.

cards.front: In Connell's barnacle removals, why was a coin toss used to choose which half of each patch got the removal?
cards.back: A person choosing by eye might pick the healthiest-looking halves for removal. Random allocation removes that bias.
cards.quote: A person choosing by eye might pick the healthiest-looking halves for the removal.
cards.section: Connell's barnacles: what the film left out

cards.front: What did Connell's removals and cages at Millport show about the lower limit of Chthamalus on the shore?
cards.back: Read together, they leave the competitor Balanus setting Chthamalus's lower limit at Millport.
cards.quote: they still leave Balanus setting Chthamalus's lower limit at Millport

cards.front: Connell caged some Millport patches to keep out the whelk Thais. If Thais ate Chthamalus directly, what result would the cages give, and what did he find?
cards.back: Chthamalus kept free of Balanus would survive worse in open patches than caged ones. He found little sign of that except at the lowest level.
cards.quote: If Thais were eating Chthamalus directly, Chthamalus kept free of Balanus would survive worse in open patches than in caged ones.

cards.front: At Millport, Thais preferred the larger barnacle Balanus. Predict how Balanus's effect on Chthamalus in caged patches compares with open patches at and below mid-tide, and why.
cards.back: Competition should be stronger in caged patches. In open patches Thais thinned Balanus, the competitor, and so weakened the competition; cages remove that thinning.
cards.why: Predation and competition interact, so cage and removal comparisons must be read together.
cards.quote: But Thais preferred the larger Balanus, so in open patches at and below mid-tide it thinned the competitor and weakened the competition.

cards.front: A barnacle removal study prods Balanus off with a needle around marked Chthamalus. What control would check that the handling itself does not change Chthamalus survival?
cards.back: A handling control: prod around Chthamalus with the needle without removing anything, and compare survival.
cards.quote: a handling control, in which you prod around Chthamalus with the needle without removing anything, would check that disturbance alone does not change survival

cards.front: Balanus excludes Chthamalus from the lower shore at Millport, yet both barnacles live on that shore. Does this contradict competitive exclusion?
cards.back: No. Exclusion in the model means loss from one place, not from everywhere; Balanus sets Chthamalus's lower limit at Millport.
cards.quote: Exclusion means loss from that one place, not from everywhere.

cards.front: Does a species' fundamental niche include the effects of its predators, such as the whelk Thais on Chthamalus?
cards.back: No. The fundamental niche excludes enemies as well as competitors, so predators belong in the realized-niche story too.
cards.quote: The fundamental niche (niches and distributions) excludes enemies as well as competitors
cards.section: Connell's barnacles: what the film left out

cards.front: {{c1::Resource partitioning}} is the division of resources among species by type, place or time.
cards.quote: Resource partitioning is the division of resources among species by type, place or time.

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra model, why does resource partitioning make coexistence easier?
cards.back: Less resource overlap can, all else equal, lower the competition coefficients, and lower alphas make it easier for each species to pass the invasion test.
cards.quote: Less resource overlap can, all else equal, lower the competition coefficients

cards.front: Two species with K1 = K2 = 100 have alpha12 = alpha21 = 1.2. Partitioning food by size lowers both alphas to 0.6. What is the outcome before and after, and where is the equilibrium after?
cards.back: Before: 100 < 120 both ways, so starting numbers decide. After: 100 > 60 both ways, stable coexistence. Equilibrium: N = (100 - 60)/(1 - 0.36) = 62.5 each.
cards.why: Lower alphas make it easier for each species to pass the invasion test.
cards.quote: in the model lower alphas make it easier for each species to pass the invasion test

cards.front: MacArthur found five warbler species foraging in different parts of the same conifer trees. Name three possible causes of such partitioning.
cards.back: Past competition driving species apart; plasticity (each shifts behaviour when the other is present); ecological sorting (only species that already differed settled together). The study was observational.
cards.quote: Robert MacArthur's 1958 study of five warbler species in northeastern conifer forests found that they foraged in different parts of the same trees.

cards.front: {{c1::Character displacement}} is evolutionary divergence between species caused by their interactions.
cards.back: Ecological character displacement: divergence in a trait caused by competition for limited resources.
cards.quote: Character displacement is evolutionary divergence between species caused by their interactions.

cards.front: What four kinds of evidence does a claim of ecological character displacement need?
cards.back: 1. The trait difference has an inherited basis. 2. The trait affects how the organism gets its resource. 3. Sorting is ruled out. 4. Competition, not another environmental change, is the cause.
cards.quote: A claim needs four kinds of evidence: The trait difference has an inherited basis, not just a response to surroundings.

cards.front: Beak size is highly heritable within one island's finch population. A researcher concludes that the beak difference between this island and another is genetic. Is the conclusion justified, and what test would support it?
cards.back: Not by itself. Heritability within one population does not show a between-population difference is genetic. A common garden, raising both in the same environment, would support it if the difference persists.
cards.quote: heritability within one population does not by itself show that a difference between populations is genetic

cards.front: Why is the Grants' study of Geospiza fortis beak change on Daphne Major a natural experiment, and what is its main weakness?
cards.back: One island, one event, no random assignment. A drought coincided with the competition, so drought is hard to separate from competition as the cause.
cards.quote: It is a natural experiment: one island, one event, no random assignment, and a drought that coincided with the competition

cards.front: Why is ecological sorting a poor explanation for the shift in G. fortis beak size on Daphne Major?
cards.back: Sorting means no species changed; the place admitted only species that already differed. Here one resident population itself changed.
cards.quote: sorting is a poor fit, because one resident population changed (item 3)

cards.front: In a drought in 1977 (before G. magnirostris arrived), selection on Daphne Major favoured large-beaked G. fortis; in 2004, with magnirostris taking the large hard seeds, it favoured small-beaked fortis. Why does this help separate competition from drought?
cards.back: The direction of selection reversed only when the competitor was present. That reversal points to competition, not drought alone.
cards.quote: That reversal points to competition, not drought alone.

cards.front: Two lizard species differ more in jaw size where they live together than where each lives alone. Outline evidence that would make this a strong case of character displacement.
cards.back: Common-garden rearing shows the jaw difference is inherited; jaw size predicts prey use; a resident population is shown to have changed (ruling out sorting); and the pattern tracks the competitor, not another environmental change.
cards.why: Rests on the four kinds of evidence; competition as the cause is the hardest to show.
cards.quote: Item 4, competition rather than drought, is the hardest.

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra competition with K1 = K2 = 100, r1 = 1.0 and r2 = 0.5 per day. An equal per-capita death rate d = 0.25 per day is added. Find the new carrying capacities.
cards.back: Each K shrinks by the fraction d/r. K1 = 100 x (1 - 0.25/1.0) = 75. K2 = 100 x (1 - 0.25/0.5) = 50. The alphas stay the same.
cards.quote: shrinks each K by the fraction d/r, more for the slow grower; the alphas stay the same

cards.front: In soil-bacteria microcosms, a slower grower wins at low dilution. Using the Lotka-Volterra coexistence conditions, explain why raising the dilution rate can reverse the winner even though r is not in the conditions.
cards.back: Dilution adds a death rate, which shrinks each K by d/r, more for the slow grower. With alphas unchanged, the slow grower's K falls relative to the fast grower's, so the conditions can flip toward the faster grower.
cards.why: r enters only through K once mortality is added; if d reaches a species' r, it cannot persist even alone.
cards.quote: Raising the dilution rate, which adds a death rate, reversed the winner.

cards.front: Two competitors both fail the invasion test. Species 1 starts at lower numbers than species 2. Can species 1 still win, and can raising its growth rate r change which start it wins from?
cards.back: Yes to both. With unequal K and alpha, the line dividing the starts each species wins from is not equal numbers, so a species can win from behind; and that line moves when growth rates change.
cards.quote: with unequal K and alpha, a species can win from behind
